## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways based on a combination of statistical significance, biological coherence, and disease relevance, and the results strongly point to inflammatory, immune, and tissue-remodeling mechanisms that are central to arthritis. Most notably, interleukin signaling (REAC:R-HSA-449147, p = 2.61 × 10−10, 39 associated proteins) and tumor necrosis factors bind their physiological receptors (REAC:R-HSA-5669034, p = 3.25 × 10−12, 13 associated proteins) were among the most significant pathways, together with cytokines and inflammatory response (WP:WP530, p = 1.40 × 10−4, 7 associated proteins) and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells transcription factor binding motif enrichment (TF:M00194_1, p = 5.10 × 10−3, 21 associated proteins). These findings are highly consistent with the literature showing that interleukins, tumor necrosis factor signaling, and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation drive synovial inflammation, leukocyte recruitment, and chronic joint damage in inflammatory arthritis, particularly rheumatoid arthritis.

Furthermore, several enriched terms support a strong role for innate and adaptive immunity. The enrichment of specific granule (GO:0042581, p = 7.88 × 10−9, 18 associated proteins) suggests neutrophil activation, which is well documented in inflamed synovial fluid and contributes to protease release, oxidative injury, and amplification of inflammation. In parallel, immunoglobulin complex (GO:0019814, p = 2.02 × 10−3, 4 associated proteins) indicates antibody-mediated immune processes, in line with evidence that autoantibodies and immune complexes contribute to complement activation and persistent synovitis in autoimmune arthritis. The direct enrichment of rheumatoid arthritis (KEGG:05323, p = 8.69 × 10−7, 14 associated proteins), arthritis (HP:0001369, p = 2.78 × 10−3, 17 associated proteins), and arthralgia (HP:0002829, p = 2.65 × 10−4, 17 associated proteins) further supports the disease specificity of this pathway set.

In addition, the data highlight extracellular matrix injury and joint structural remodeling as major components of disease biology. Extracellular matrix structural constituent (GO:0005201, p = 1.88 × 10−7, 17 associated proteins), extracellular matrix disassembly (GO:0022617, p = 1.53 × 10−6, 10 associated proteins), matrix metalloproteinases (WP:WP129, p = 2.45 × 10−4, 7 associated proteins), and cell adhesion molecules (KEGG:04514, p = 2.16 × 10−7, 19 associated proteins) collectively suggest active degradation of cartilage and connective tissue, together with enhanced leukocyte adhesion and migration into the joint. This pattern agrees with extensive literature showing that matrix metalloproteinase-driven matrix breakdown and adhesion molecule-mediated immune cell infiltration are key mechanisms underlying pannus formation, cartilage erosion, and progressive joint destruction.

Finally, enrichment of osteoblast differentiation (GO:0001649, p = 1.53 × 10−5, 14 associated proteins) indicates altered bone remodeling, which is also a recognized feature of arthritis, where inflammatory mediators disrupt the balance between bone formation and bone resorption. Overall, the highly significant p-values across inflammatory signaling, neutrophil granule biology, antibody-associated immunity, extracellular matrix turnover, and bone differentiation support a model in which arthritis is driven by coordinated cytokine-dependent immune activation and progressive destruction of joint tissue, a conclusion that is strongly supported by the current biomedical literature.
